title: Type-safe generic classes
idea: Generics let one class work for many types while the compiler checks each use, so callers never cast and wrong types fail at compile time.
points: The class declares a type parameter `T`; each caller picks the actual type.
A bound such as `T extends Entity<ID>` lets the class call `id()` safely.
Take `? extends T` to read items in, `? super T` to write out.
Type arguments are erased at runtime, so `new T()` does not compile.

hero.title: One generic repository, many entity types

steps.caption: `Repository` declares two type parameters: the id type and the entity type.
The bound says `T` must be an `Entity<ID>`, so the code may call `id()`.
`User` and `Order` implement `Entity` with different id types.
`InMemoryRepository` is written once against `ID` and `T`, never a concrete class.
`users` fixes `ID=String, T=User`. `findById` now returns `Optional<User>`, no cast.
`orders` reuses the same class with other types. Saving a `User` there fails to compile.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: An `Object` store: every read needs a cast, and a wrong type crashes at runtime.

walk.text: The store holds `Object`, so the compiler cannot know what is inside.
A `String` is accepted where a `User` was meant. Nothing flags it.
Every caller casts. This one is right, by luck rather than by type.
The wrong value surfaces only when read, far from where it was stored.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: A bounded generic repository with `Optional` reads and wildcard bulk methods.

walk.text: `Entity<ID>` is the bound. Each record states its own id type.
The contract is generic too, so any caller gets typed results.
`T extends Entity<ID>` lets `save` call `item.id()` with no cast.
`Optional<T>` makes a missing row explicit instead of returning `null`.
`? extends T` reads from producers; `? super T` writes into consumers.
One class serves users and orders. The commented line would not compile.

pitfalls: Using raw types like `List` without a parameter: errors move from compile time to runtime.
Taking `List<T>` when callers have `List<Subtype>`: use `? extends T` for inputs.
Adding type parameters nobody varies makes signatures noisy; generify only real variation.

quiz.q: Given `copyTo(Collection<? super T> target)` on a repository of `User`, which call compiles?
quiz.why: `? super User` accepts `User` or any supertype, such as `Object`. `User` is an `Entity<String>`, so `Entity<Integer>` and `String` are not supertypes.

takeaway: Let the caller pick the type; let the compiler stop the wrong one.

starters: When should a method be generic rather than the whole class?
